name: Horse oil
lead: Horse oil (ma-yu in Japanese and Korean cosmetic usage) is a fat rendered from horse tissue, used as an emollient ingredient in skin-care products, particularly in East Asia. Its fatty-acid profile, including linoleic and palmitoleic acids, has been described as similar to that of human skin lipids.[1]

Evidence consists of small formulation and laboratory studies, including work from Korean research groups on microneedle patches and on cultured skin cells. No independent clinical trial in people was found.
infobox: Linoleic, palmitoleic and other unsaturated fatty acids

paras: Mid-twentieth-century biochemical studies analysed the fatty acids of horse depot fat, muscle and liver, and compared horse oil with fats from other pasture-fed animals.[2][3] A 2018 study notes it contains unsaturated fatty acids similar to those in human skin and used it as a starting material for producing sophorolipid biosurfactants for cosmetics.[1]

A 2018 study in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology developed dissolving microneedle patches loaded with horse oil, reporting skin-barrier restoration and moisturisation in its tests.[4] A 2019 study combined horse oil and adenosine in a two-phase patch and reported moisturisation and wrinkle improvement.[5] A 2019 laboratory study reported that horse oil reduced UVB-induced oxidative damage in human HaCaT keratinocytes.[6] Formulation work has examined emulsion stability.[7]

No dedicated clinical trials of topical horse oil were found beyond the small formulation studies above, which tested patches in limited settings and were authored by the groups developing them.[4][5] A rat study compared horse oil with other oils for cholesterol effects, which is unrelated to skin.[8]
A 2025 analytical study developed an infrared-spectroscopy method to detect adulteration of horse oil, indicating that authenticity of commercial products is an active concern for researchers.[9]

card.summary: An animal-derived emollient oil from Japanese and Korean skin care, backed by small formulation and cell studies only.
card.note: Studies are small and mostly by developers; no independent human trials found.

quick.overview:
Horse oil is a fat from horses used as an emollient in some Japanese and Korean skin-care products. Makers point to its fatty acids resembling those in human skin.

Research is limited to small formulation, cell and patch studies; no independent clinical trial was found.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an emollient supplying unsaturated fatty acids; lab work reports barrier-supporting and antioxidant effects in cultured keratinocytes.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to people were found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived product, and researchers have studied methods for detecting adulterated oil.
